extracted.intended_audience: urban planners, municipal engineers, architects, and informed readers interested in city design and street layout
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for laying out streets and planning the development of cities, balancing geometric efficiency, population distribution, geography, climate, economy, and historical constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectangular (grid) street system — advantages and disadvantages
rubrics_metrics.description: The rectangular system of laying out streets has the advantage of extreme simplicity, and lends itself to a convenient adjustment of the interior of the houses of a city; but it is monotonous in the extreme, and makes communication between one quarter of the town and another very inconvenient; for the passenger is compelled to go along the two sides of a triangle to accomplish the distance represented by its hypotenuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use grid for simplicity and convenient house plans; avoid when through-travel efficiency and variety are priorities. The grid is an anti-pattern where direct diagonal movement is frequent. Consider mixing with diagonal or radial streets to reduce travel inefficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit planning objectives: minimize wasted space and shorten major communication lines
rubrics_metrics.description: By what law can we arrange the streets so as to lose the least possible amount of space, and still have the greatest possible length of roads; and, given a surface of which the shape and area are known, and the law of the division of the population having been ascertained, how shall we lay out the roads so as to make the different lines of communication, particularly the most frequented ones, as short as possible?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat planning as an optimization problem: balance land consumption, amount/length of roads, and shortest paths for high-traffic routes. Use population distribution ('law of the division of the population') to prioritize which connections must be shortest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of geometric plan (square/hexagonal/octagonal/circular)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four plans ordinarily present themselves ... the square, hexagonal, octagonal, and circular. Of these, the hexagonal type seems, according to our mathematical calculations, the one which gives the greatest length of streets and the greatest amount of habitable surface, with the smallest consumption of space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer hexagonal layouts when objective is to maximize street length and habitable area per land used. Octagonal and hexagonal are preferable to square for homogeneous populations (better utilization and communication). Use circular plans where population density decreases from center outward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid impractical lot shapes (acute angles) as a design objection
rubrics_metrics.description: Both plans are liable to the objection that they give house-lots having acute angles of sixty degrees in the hexagonal, and of forty-five degrees in the octagonal plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh geometric efficiencies against practical lot usability; acute-angled house-lots are a recognized drawback of hex/oct plans. Where lot shape practicality is important, modify geometry or combine plans to reduce acute angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use circular plan for cities with radial density gradients
rubrics_metrics.description: Practically the population finds it convenient to bear toward the center of the city, and, the more it bears that way, the more it is to its interest to do so. Consequently, the density of the population diminishes from the center toward the circumference. Under such conditions, the circular plan is very satisfactory. It has in effect the double advantage of furnishing direct roads to the center of the town, and of accommodating itself to giving to the houses in the outlying quarters the greater amount of space they require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt circular or concentric arrangements when centralization (people bearing toward center) and decreasing outer density are present. Circular layouts give direct radial access to center and permit larger lots in outskirts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design central zone with hexagonal core, boulevards, and radial/suburban transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: For the center of cities, where the population is compact and homogeneous, where land is dear and communication is needed in every direction alike, the hexagonal plan, with the reservation of a few places for public monuments, is most convenient. This central part might be surrounded by a boulevard, beyond which the circular type might be adopted with modifications so as to avoid curved streets. The principal streets of each suburb might be directed toward the center of the city, and each suburb might in itself be laid out more or less according to the rectangular type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine geometries: hexagonal central core with reserved monument sites, encircling boulevard, modified circular suburbs, and rectangular layouts within suburbs; ensure principal suburban streets are radial toward center. Use diagonal/main arteries crossing the city to link distant quarters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for topography and fixed physical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain directions in the ways of communication are often imposed by the topographical situation; as, for example, when the town is crossed by a river or a highway. Some cities are free to extend over the plain in any direction, while others are restricted to narrow valleys, or to islands of which they cover the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let rivers, existing highways, valleys, and islands shape street directions. In constrained sites (islands, narrow valleys), accept narrow/crooked streets as necessary adaptations (examples: Cadiz, St. Malo, Venice). Avoid forcing ideal geometry where topography forbids it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate and ventilation considerations in street geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrow and crooked streets protect the inhabitants against heat and against cold, but they foster the accumulation of miasms and prevent the circulation of air. Cities tend to expand on the side from which the prevailing winds come. It is the most pleasant side, because it is free from the unhealthy emanations of the town.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance thermal protection with ventilation and sanitation: narrow/crooked streets may moderate temperature extremes but harm air circulation and public health. Orient expansion considering prevailing winds to place cleaner, more desirable areas upwind. Use boulevard or wider streets where ventilation is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economical principle: street width proportional to traffic and align with commercial currents
rubrics_metrics.description: In considering the economical side, account must be taken of the density of the population and the frequency of communications. It is important that the principal centers be connected by wide, direct, and easy roads following the course of the most usual commercial currents. Theoretically, the width of each street should be proportionate to the traffic upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate street widths and hierarchy according to expected traffic volumes: principal arteries wide and direct along commercial flows; minor streets narrower. Prioritize connectivity between principal centers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect historical and existing urban fabric when introducing new streets
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical considerations may sometimes rule, for due force must be allowed to existing conditions in the construction of each new street.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modifying or adding streets, accommodate existing historic layouts, axes, and usage patterns; do not ignore legacy streets and monuments. Use gradual modification rather than wholesale replacement when history dictates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and plan for different development processes (open vs fortified cities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open cities generally expand gradually by the building of houses along the roads toward neighboring towns ... Fortified cities are developed in an intermittent way. After having been for a long time smothered within their walls, they end by breaking the barriers down and uniting with their suburbs; constructing elegant boulevards in the places formerly occupied by their fortifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate different growth morphologies: allow radiated/palmate forms for open cities (favorable to communications); plan for concentric ring/boulevard development when fortifications are removed. Use these expectations to plan future transport and services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and leverage the historic grand artery and central functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Most frequently the old town is traversed by a grand artery, the history of which goes back to the origin of the place, and which is usually busy with trade and much crowded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and maintain major historic thoroughfares as they often continue to serve as primary commercial and circulation axes. Reinforce these with appropriate widths, transit options, and connections to suburbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suburban form: lower density requires different street spacing and convergence to center
rubrics_metrics.description: The population of the suburbs is generally less dense than that of the city proper; and the streets are wider, and the houses farther apart. The inhabitants of the suburbs are in the habit of going frequently to the center of the city ... The principal streets of the suburbs also converge toward the center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design suburbs with wider spacing and larger lots; ensure principal suburban streets are radial and provide efficient access to the center. Reduce transverse street frequency as distance from center increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reconstruction and urban renewal to improve hygiene and street order where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: At other times the hand of man destroys entire quarters, to reconstruct them in a more convenient and more hygienic manner. In such cases the worst quarters are the first to suffer transformation, and become in their turn the most elegant ones. The example set in Paris, under the administration of M. Haussmann, has been extensively followed in other cities in France and abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When undertaking reconstruction (after fires or through renewal), prioritize sanitary improvements, wider streets, and better circulation; often start with worst quarters. Use such opportunities to implement boulevards and regularized street patterns but weigh against displacement and historic preservation concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider maritime and infrastructural works (basins, ports) as drivers of major street-grouping changes
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction of new basins in sea-ports also frequently leads to radical modifications of the aspect of the towns and in the grouping of their streets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning coastal or port cities, integrate expected maritime infrastructure (basins, docks) into the street layout; anticipate that such works will reshape urban blocks and circulation and plan accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: General judgment: rectangular grid is imperfect; use mixed, context-driven solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: We are evidently very far from exhausting the questions that grow out of the subject; but we hope we have succeeded in showing how complex and interesting they are, and how imperfect is the plan of those cities that are laid out in a network of rectangular streets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not default to a single template (grid). Choose hybrid solutions that respond to geometric efficiency, population patterns, climate, topography, economy, and historical context; combine hexagonal, circular, radial, and rectangular elements as appropriate.
